```plato

    // The two bodies after one visit to a ball-and-socket: its three axes solved in
    // turn, each seeing what the previous one wrote. The swing and twist limits the
    // type declares are NOT enforced — they are orientation constraints, and this
    // file solves only positional ones.
    SolveJoint(bodies: Array<SolverBody3D>, joint: BallSocketJoint, stiffness: Number,
        seconds: Number): Array<SolverBody3D>
    {
        var afterX = SolveBallSocketAxis(bodies, joint, Vector3D(1.0, 0.0, 0.0), stiffness, seconds);
        var afterY = SolveBallSocketAxis(afterX, joint, Vector3D(0.0, 1.0, 0.0), stiffness, seconds);
        return SolveBallSocketAxis(afterY, joint, Vector3D(0.0, 0.0, 1.0), stiffness, seconds);
    }

    //==
    // # Springs
    //
    // A spring joint is not a constraint: it exerts a FORCE and lets the integrator
    // decide what happens. That is why it takes a time step and produces an impulse
    // rather than being iterated — iterating a spring would multiply its stiffness
    // by the iteration count.
    //
    // A spring stiff enough to look rigid is stiff enough to be unstable at the
    // step sizes a real-time simulation uses; a joint that must be rigid should be
    // a `DistanceJoint` with equal bounds instead.

    // The force the spring exerts along the line between its anchors, in newtons,
    // signed so that a positive value pushes the anchors apart: Hooke's restoring
    // term plus a damping term proportional to the rate of change of the length.
    // (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hooke%27s_law)
    SpringForce(joint: SpringJoint, extension: Number, lengthRate: Number): Number
        => -joint.Stiffness.Amount * extension - joint.Damping.Amount * lengthRate;

    // The two bodies after a spring has acted for one step: the spring force turned
    // into an impulse by multiplying by the step, and applied at the two anchors.
    // Coincident anchors have no line of action and the spring does nothing.
    ApplySpring(bodies: Array<SolverBody3D>, joint: SpringJoint, seconds: Number): Array<SolverBody3D>
    {
        var a = bodies[joint.BodyA.Value];
        var b = bodies[joint.BodyB.Value];
        var anchorA = WorldAnchor(a, joint.AnchorA);
        var anchorB = WorldAnchor(b, joint.AnchorB);
        var span = anchorA.Between(anchorB);
        var separation = span.Magnitude;
        var axis = separation > 0.0 ? span / separation : Vector3D(0.0, 0.0, 1.0);
        var impulse = separation <= 0.0
            ? 0.0
            : SpringForce(joint, separation - joint.RestLength.Amount,
                SeparationSpeed(a, b, anchorA, anchorB, axis)) * seconds;
        return ReplacedAt(
            ReplacedAt(bodies, joint.BodyA.Value, ApplyImpulse(a, axis * -impulse, anchorA)),
            joint.BodyB.Value,
            ApplyImpulse(b, axis * impulse, anchorB));
    }

    //==
    // # Solving a set of joints
    //
    // The same fold the contact solver uses, over an array of joints instead of an
    // array of contact rows: one pass visits every joint once in order, and the
    // solve runs a fixed number of passes. Joints and contacts converge together
    // when their passes are interleaved; running all the joint passes and then all
    // the contact passes lets the contacts undo the joints, which reads as a
    // ragdoll whose limbs stretch on the frames it lands.

    // One pass over every distance joint.
    SolveDistanceJointPass(bodies: Array<SolverBody3D>, joints: Array<DistanceJoint>,
        stiffness: Number, seconds: Number): Array<SolverBody3D>
        => joints.Reduce(bodies, (acc, joint) => SolveJoint(acc, joint, stiffness, seconds));

    // One pass over every ball-and-socket joint.
    SolveBallSocketJointPass(bodies: Array<SolverBody3D>, joints: Array<BallSocketJoint>,
        stiffness: Number, seconds: Number): Array<SolverBody3D>
        => joints.Reduce(bodies, (acc, joint) => SolveJoint(acc, joint, stiffness, seconds));

    // `iterations` passes over both joint kinds, distance joints first. The
    // ordering is arbitrary and it matters: Gauss-Seidel converges to the same
    // answer either way, but reaches it along a different path, so a simulation is
    // reproducible only against a fixed order.
    SolveJoints(bodies: Array<SolverBody3D>, distanceJoints: Array<DistanceJoint>,
        ballSocketJoints: Array<BallSocketJoint>, iterations: Integer, stiffness: Number,
        seconds: Number): Array<SolverBody3D>
        => Indices(iterations).Reduce(bodies, (acc, i) =>
            SolveBallSocketJointPass(
                SolveDistanceJointPass(acc, distanceJoints, stiffness, seconds),
                ballSocketJoints, stiffness, seconds));
}
```
